title: Reuse clusterization and bandwidth serialization diary
content:
Summary:
This is a working notebook capturing exploratory profiling around two related phenomena we keep seeing in prod traces: (1) tight clusters of repeated KV block reuse across short windows (we call these "reuse clusters"), and (2) serializing effects on memory-channel bandwidth when these clusters are served concurrently, which amplifies paging and eviction churn. Goal is to characterize the interaction and produce reproducible microbenchmarks that isolate bandwidth serialization.

Motivation / why this matters:
- Observed sudden latency spikes on tail when multiple hot sessions overlap (same hotset but different model shards).
- Eviction churn increases sharply even when overall resident set size should be sufficient; hypothesis is that channel-level serialization causes effective lowering of throughput per NVMe/DRAM channel, triggering more pageouts.
- If true, mitigation options differ: scheduler/placement vs eviction heuristics vs per-session backpressure.

Measurement setup (machines and traces):
- Target host: p4d.24xlarge-style (8 x A100-like), NUMA nodes: 2, memory channels: 6 per socket.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main + perf counters (PR 367) enabling per-request residency sampling and trace_id tagging.
- Workloads: two synthetic workloads derived from prod trace slices:
  * cluster-A: short-context chat workload, dense reuse of bottom 2 layers' KV for first 4 tokens (hotset size ~120MB).
  * cluster-B: long-context summarization workload, sparse reuse but high KV-request rate later in sequence (hotset size ~260MB).
- Tools: perf, nvprof/nsight, custom eBPF trace for LRU evict calls, and kernel slab+pagealloc stats.
- Key metrics collected: per-socket DRAM bandwidth (B/s), per-channel queue depth, page-in/sec, eviction/sec (LRU calls), median & 99.9th latency for generate_token path.

What I ran (commands / harness):
- Harness script: experiments/bandwidth_serialization/run.sh --scale 4 --mix cluster-a:3,cluster-b:2 --pin-sockets 0,1 --enable-residency-sampling
- perf sample command: sudo perf stat -e cpu-cycles,cache-misses,LLC-loads -p $PID -I 1000
- nvprof collect: NSIGHT_TRACE=1 ./serve --trace-nsight --trace-id $TRACE
- eBPF collection: sudo ./ebpf/trace_lru --pid $PID --out lru_events.log

Observations (raw):
- When two cluster-A sessions overlap on the same socket, DRAM bandwidth per-session drops ~30% compared to sequential runs, while aggregate stays roughly constant.
- Page-in/sec rises by ~2.1x during overlap windows; eviction/sec also increases but with ~150ms lag.
- 99.9th token latency shows ~2.5x inflation in overlap windows, but median unaffected.
- Nsight traces show long stretches where a single memory channel queue is saturated while others have lower utilization — not perfectly balanced distribution of large KV reads.
- Residency samples show short-lived resident spikes: many blocks are promoted (touch) then evicted within <700ms which matches the bursty access patterns.

Interpretation / hypotheses (ranked):
1) Channel serialization hypothesis (primary): The runtime's current page placement and dma-stride cause multiple concurrent streams to align on the same memory channel, saturating it and forcing the OS/hardware to serialize large transfers, increasing latency and causing reactive evictions.
2) Hotset fragmentation hypothesis: Hot blocks are dispersed across many pages and page boundary misalignment increases read amplification, producing uneven channel pressure.
3) Scheduler interference: Thread-to-socket pinning and our batching behavior create synchronized bursts causing simultaneous large KV reads instead of smooth spreading.
4) Eviction policy lag: The LRU window is too coarse; when reuse clusters appear, eviction daemon reacts too slowly and starts evicting still-hot blocks.

Quick microbench ideas to isolate channel effects:
- Controlled allocator run: allocate hotset with explicit hugepage alignment to force even channel distribution, compare bandwidth skew.
- Staggered micro-launch: offset start times of sessions by 50ms to see if tail reduces (tests scheduler hypothesis).
- Synthetic channel hammer: small program that issues aligned read patterns to reproduce single-channel saturation.

Experiments done and results (concise):
- Hugepage alignment test: aligning hotset reduced single-channel peak by ~40% and dropped 99.9th latency by ~18% in cluster-A overlap; suggests fragmentation contributes but not the whole story.
- Staggered starts: offsetting by 100ms reduced latency peaks ~25% — indicates scheduler synchronization is a factor.
- Eviction daemon tune: lowered recheck interval to 50ms; eviction/sec smoothed but page-in/sec stayed high, tail latency slightly improved.

Notes on reproducibility and flaky signals:
- Repro is sensitive to background NVMe activity and kernel updates; collect baseline using idle run for 30s prior to each test.
- eBPF trace introduces ~3–5% overhead; keep runs long enough to amortize (>=120s).

Potential mitigations being prototyped locally:
- Placement shim: a lightweight allocator stage that biases hotset placement across channels using hugepage offsets (prototype in alloc/placement-experiments).
- Request jittering: introduce small per-request randomized delays in batch scheduler to de-synchronize bursts (config flag: serve.jitter_ms).
- Eviction prediction: fast TTL for blocks touched >N times in window; prefer demotion instead of eviction during suspected cluster windows.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Does getting more granular (per-channel) kernel telemetry materially change our view? Can we export metrics via PMU counters?
- How does multi-tenant (3+ workloads) change interactions — are effects linear or superlinear?
- Can we detect reuse clusters at admission time cheaply (probabilistic sketch) and apply targeted placement/backpressure?

Next steps (actionable):
- [Aisha] finish allocator prototype and benchmark (ETA 1 week).
- [Marcus] add PMU per-channel counters to perf harness (ETA 3 days).
- [Sofia] run multi-tenant sweep with 3 workload mixes and collect long traces (ETA 1 week).
- Schedule follow-up deep-dive with infra and runtime schedulers (invite: @infra-team, @runtime-team).

Notes-to-self (short):
- Put synthetic single-channel hammer in perf-ci so we can detect regressions in CI.
- Cross-reference with INF-701 (eviction telemetry) before changing eviction heuristics broadly.

Appendix: useful extract from an overlap trace (redacted):
- trace_id: TRACE-20240513-1142
- overlap window: 2024-05-13T11:42:12.341Z -> 2024-05-13T11:42:18.912Z
- per-socket DRAM B/s: socket0: 42GB/s -> 28GB/s (per-session drop), socket1: 37GB/s -> 36GB/s
- page-in/sec: 420 -> 920 during window
- 99.9th latency: 11.3ms -> 28.6ms

If anyone reads this and wants to take a slice: look at alloc/placement-experiments/hugepage-align/README.md for the allocator prototype; it contains the exact script used for the hugepage test plus raw nsight outputs.
